Chapter 1Problem Introduction

1.1 The problem in one paragraph

Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT can write fluent answers to almost any question, but they have two weaknesses that matter a lot in real work. First, they only know what was in their training data, so they know nothing about your documents: a company policy, a lecture PDF, a signed contract, a patient report. Second, when they do not know something they often hallucinate, which means they produce a confident, well-written answer that is simply false. A model that sounds sure but is wrong is worse than no model at all, because the reader has no way to notice the mistake.

Askmargin is the NLP application built in this project to address both weaknesses. The user gives it a set of PDF documents and asks a question in plain English. Askmargin finds the passages of the documents that are most relevant to the question, writes a short answer using only those passages, and shows the page number where the evidence was found. If the documents do not contain the answer, it says so instead of guessing. The name comes from the habit of writing a note in the margin of a page: every answer points back to a page.

The technique used is called Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Instead of asking the model to answer from memory, we first retrieve relevant text from a document collection and then let the model generate an answer from that text. RAG is currently the most common way in which companies connect an LLM to private data.

1.2 Why plain LLMs hallucinate

A language model is trained to predict the next word. It learns patterns of language and a large amount of world knowledge, but this knowledge is stored loosely inside its weights and is not looked up the way a database record is. Three things follow from this:

  • Knowledge is frozen. Anything that happened after the training date, or anything that was never public (internal reports, personal files), is unknown to the model.
  • There is no built-in "I do not know". The model always produces the most likely next words, so for an unknown fact it produces a plausible-sounding guess.
  • There is no source. The answer cannot be checked because the model cannot say where it learnt a fact.

RAG attacks all three: the knowledge lives in a document store that can be updated at any time, the model is told to use only the supplied text, and each supplied chunk carries its page number, which becomes the citation.

1.3 Real-world applications

The same pipeline (split documents, search them by meaning, answer from the best passages, cite the source) is used in many industries:

Domain Typical question Why RAG fits
Enterprise search "What is our laptop replacement policy for new joiners?" Thousands of wikis, PDFs and slide decks that keyword search handles poorly; answers must follow the current version of a policy.
Customer support "How do I reset the router to factory settings?" Answers must come from the manual of the exact product, and a wrong instruction costs money.
Legal "What is the notice period in clause 14 of this agreement?" Lawyers need the exact clause and page, not a summary from memory.
Medical "What dose adjustment does this guideline recommend for kidney patients?" Guidelines change; the answer must cite the approved document and refuse when it is not covered.
Education "Explain the difference between BERT and Sentence-BERT from my notes." A study assistant that answers from the student's own material and tells them which page to re-read.
Research "Which optimiser did the paper use?" Quick lookup inside long papers, as demonstrated by the corpus of this project.

In legal and medical settings a refusal is as important as a correct answer. A system that answers "I could not find this in the documents" when the question is out of scope is safer than one that always answers. This is why refusal is a first-class feature of Askmargin and is evaluated separately.

1.4 Objectives of the project

  1. Choose a real-world NLP task (document question answering) and a public dataset (four open-access research papers).
  2. Implement every stage of the pipeline ourselves in Python: text extraction and cleaning, tokenisation, stop-word removal, lemmatisation, chunking, TF-IDF, BM25, dense sentence embeddings, a vector store with cosine similarity and FAISS, a refusal rule, and answer generation with an open model.
  3. Evaluate honestly on a hand-written test set of 30 questions, using Recall@k, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and answer-level checks, and compare design choices (retrieval method, chunking strategy, chunk size).
  4. Show the result as a working web demo at askmargin.vercel.app.

Everything runs on free tools (PyMuPDF, NLTK, scikit-learn, rank-bm25, Sentence-Transformers, FAISS, FLAN-T5 through Hugging Face Transformers) on a laptop CPU or free Google Colab, so every number in this report can be reproduced.

Chapter 2Dataset and Evaluation Set

2.1 The document collection

The task needs "private documents" that anyone can obtain, so that every result can be reproduced. We use four open-access research papers from arXiv, downloaded automatically by the notebook (Step 1). All four are about NLP, which allowed us to write questions whose answers can be checked by reading the paper.

Table 2.1: The corpus, as counted by the notebook after cleaning (pages with fewer than 80 characters are skipped).
Key Paper arXiv id Pages used Words
attention Attention Is All You Need (the Transformer) 1706.03762 15 6,072
bert BERT: pre-training of deep bidirectional transformers 1810.04805 16 9,828
rag Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks 2005.11401 19 9,839
sbert Sentence-BERT 1908.10084 11 6,440
Total 61 32,179

Choosing papers about the very topic of the project has a pleasant side effect: the corpus is a realistic example of "long technical documents with numbers, tables and equations", which is the hard case for retrieval. It also means a reader of this report can open the PDFs and verify any answer.

2.2 Chunks produced

After cleaning, the pages are cut into chunks (Section 3.4). The fixed-size strategy (500 characters, 100 overlap) produced 552 chunks with an average length of 479.7 characters. The sentence-aware strategy (500 characters target) produced 717 chunks with an average of 429.6 characters (minimum 54, maximum 820, because a single long sentence can exceed the target). Each chunk stores three things: the paper key, the page number and the text.

2.3 The 30-question evaluation set

The questions were written by hand (file eval_questions.json). There are 25 answerable questions (8 about the Transformer, 7 about BERT, 5 about RAG, 5 about Sentence-BERT) and 5 out-of-document questions that no paper answers. For each answerable question we store:

  • the paper it belongs to,
  • an answer string that appears literally in the paper (used to decide whether a retrieved chunk is a hit), and
  • an expected key phrase (such as 8, 15% or FAISS) that must appear in the generated answer.

A chunk is a hit only if it is from the right paper and contains the answer string after both are lower-cased and stripped of punctuation. The notebook checks that with both chunking strategies the answer string is present in at least one chunk for 25 of 25 questions, so a perfect retriever could score 100% and no question is impossible because of chunking. The five out-of-document questions (capital of France, football world cup 2022, a cake recipe, the price of a Tesla Model 3, the prime minister of India) test the refusal rule.

Chapter 3Pipeline: Step by Step

3.1 Overview

The pipeline has two halves. In the indexing half (run once per document set) the PDFs are read, cleaned, cut into chunks and turned into vectors that are stored. In the question-answering half (run for every question) the question is turned into a vector with the same model, the closest chunks are retrieved, a refusal check decides whether the document can answer at all, and finally a language model writes a short answer from the retrieved text. An offline evaluation step measures how good each choice is.

Table 3.1: Stage-to-technique map of the notebook.
Step Stage Technique Notebook step
1-2 Extraction and cleaning PyMuPDF text extraction, Unicode NFKC, regex clean-up Step 2
2b Text preprocessing for lexical search Lower-casing, regex tokenisation, stop-word removal, WordNet lemmatisation Step 3
3 Chunking Fixed window with overlap vs sentence-aware packing Step 4
4 Vectorisation TF-IDF, BM25, dense MiniLM embeddings Step 6
5 Vector store NumPy matrix and FAISS IndexFlatIP, cosine similarity Step 7
8 Retrieval Top-k by score; hybrid fusion (RRF) Steps 6, 8
9 Refusal threshold Cut-off on best cosine score Step 9
10 Generation Prompt template with context, FLAN-T5-base Step 10
11 Evaluation Recall@k, MRR, answer / citation / faithfulness / refusal Steps 8, 11

3.2 Text extraction and cleaning

PDFs do not store paragraphs; they store characters at positions on a page. PyMuPDF (fitz) reads the characters of each page and returns them as a string. We process one page at a time and keep the page number, because it becomes the citation later. The raw text has typical problems, which clean() fixes: (a) ligatures such as the single character "ﬁ" are converted to "fi" with Unicode NFKC normalisation; (b) words split by a hyphen at the end of a line ("repre-\nsentation") are re-joined with a regular expression; (c) line breaks and repeated spaces become single spaces. Pages with fewer than 80 characters (blank or figure-only pages) are skipped.

3.3 Tokenisation, stop-words and lemmatisation

TF-IDF and BM25 compare words, so the text must first be turned into a clean list of word tokens. This is the classical NLP pre-processing chain taught in class:

  1. Lower-casing so "Model" and "model" are the same word.
  2. Tokenisation with the regular expression [a-z0-9]+, which splits on spaces and punctuation and keeps numbers (numbers matter here: "8 heads", "15%").
  3. Stop-word removal using the NLTK English list, dropping very common words ("the", "of", "is") that carry little meaning.
  4. Lemmatisation with the WordNet lemmatiser, which maps a word to its dictionary form ("layers" becomes "layer"). We use lemmatisation instead of stemming because it always returns real words.

Worked example (real notebook output). The sentence "The encoder is composed of a stack of N = 6 identical layers." becomes the tokens ['encoder', 'composed', 'stack', 'identical', 'layer']: "the", "is", "of", "a" are stop-words, and the one-character tokens "n" and "6" are dropped because the tokeniser keeps only tokens longer than one character (so single-digit numbers are lost in the lexical baselines, a small weakness of this pre-processing).

The dense embedding model does not use this chain: a transformer reads the raw sentence, including stop-words, because words like "not" change meaning.

3.4 Chunking

An embedding model and a generator can only read a limited amount of text, and a full page mixes many topics, so each page is cut into chunks. Two strategies are compared:

  • Fixed-size chunking. A window of 500 characters slides over the page text in steps of 400 (overlap of 100 characters). It is simple but may cut a sentence in the middle.
  • Sentence-aware chunking. The page is split into sentences with NLTK's Punkt tokenizer. Whole sentences are packed into a chunk until adding another would exceed 500 characters; the last sentence is then repeated at the start of the next chunk (one-sentence overlap), so the context is not lost at the boundary.

Why overlap? If an answer sentence sits exactly on a cut, a chunk without overlap would hold only half of it and neither half would match the question well; repeating 100 characters (or one sentence) gives the boundary text a second chance to be retrieved. Chunks never cross a page boundary, so every chunk has exactly one page number. A later ablation tests chunk sizes of 250, 500, 800 and 1200 characters.

3.5 Turning text into vectors

A computer cannot compare sentences directly; it compares numbers. Three representations are used.

TF-IDF. Each chunk becomes a long vector with one position per vocabulary word. The value is the product of how often the word appears in the chunk (term frequency) and how rare it is in all chunks (inverse document frequency):

wt,d = tft,d × idft,   idft = ln 1 + N1 + dft + 1

where N is the number of chunks and dft is the number of chunks containing term t (the smoothed formula used by scikit-learn). A word that appears in every chunk gets a small weight; a rare, specific word such as "FAISS" gets a large one.

BM25. BM25 is the formula used by classic search engines. It improves TF-IDF with saturation (the tenth occurrence of a word adds less than the second) and length normalisation (a long chunk should not win just because it has more words):

score(q,d) = ∑t ∈ q idft · tft,d (k1 + 1)tft,d + k1 (1 − b + b · |d| / avgdl)

with the usual defaults k1 and b of the rank-bm25 library.

Dense embeddings. The model all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (a Sentence-BERT model) turns any text into a vector of 384 numbers so that texts with similar meaning get nearby vectors, even if they share no words. This lets "How many layers..." match "a stack of N = 6 identical layers". The embeddings are normalised to length 1.

3.6 Vector store and cosine similarity

Retrieval means finding the chunk vectors closest to the question vector. We use the cosine similarity, the cosine of the angle between two vectors:

cos(q, d) = q · d‖q‖ ‖d‖ = ∑i qi di√(∑qi2) √(∑di2)

Because our vectors have length 1, the denominator is 1 and cosine similarity is just a dot product, so searching the whole store is one matrix-vector multiplication (E @ v). The "vector store" is therefore a NumPy matrix with one row per chunk. We also build a FAISS IndexFlatIP (inner-product index), which does the same exact search in optimised C++ and is the structure that real systems scale up from; the notebook asserts that FAISS and NumPy return the same top results. Worked example: for the question "How many parallel attention heads does the Transformer use?" both return chunks 21, 46 and 22 with cosine scores 0.697, 0.696 and 0.637. A score near 1 means the same meaning and a score near 0 means unrelated text; this is also why a single cut-off on the best score can separate answerable from unanswerable questions (Section 3.8).

3.7 Retrieval methods compared

Four retrievers are compared on the same chunks: TF-IDF (cosine between sparse vectors), BM25, Dense (MiniLM), and a Hybrid that merges the BM25 ranking and the dense ranking with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). In RRF each chunk receives, from every ranking it appears in, a score of

RRF(d) = ∑r 1k + rankr(d),   k = 60

and chunks are sorted by the total. A chunk that is high in both lists wins, which combines exact word matching with meaning matching.

3.8 Refusal threshold

Retrieval always returns something, even for the question "What is the capital of France?" over four NLP papers. To avoid answering from irrelevant text, the system looks at the best cosine score. If it is below a threshold T, the system refuses with "I could not find this in the documents" and never calls the generator. T is chosen by scanning candidate values from 0.10 to 0.70 and keeping the one that best separates the answerable questions (high best-score) from the out-of-document ones (low best-score); the accept/refuse accuracy is reported in Chapter 5.

3.9 Generation with FLAN-T5

If the question passes the gate, the top 3 chunks are placed into a prompt template that tells the model to answer briefly, use only the context, and reply "I don't know." otherwise. The generator is FLAN-T5-base (about 250 million parameters), an instruction-tuned encoder-decoder model with open weights that runs on a CPU. Decoding uses beam search with 4 beams and at most 64 new tokens. Importantly, the citation is not produced by the model: the page numbers of the two best chunks are copied from the chunk metadata, so a citation can never be invented.

3.10 Evaluation metrics

A retrieved chunk counts as a hit for a question if it comes from the right paper and contains the stored answer string (compared after removing punctuation and case). With Q answerable questions:

Recall@k = 1|Q| ∑q ∈ Q 𝟙[ rankq ≤ k ],    MRR = 1|Q| ∑q ∈ Q 1rankq

where rankq is the position of the first hit for question q (the reciprocal rank is 0 if no hit is found in the top 5). Recall@k answers "is the evidence in the top k?", MRR rewards putting it first. For the full answers four more checks are used: answer correct (the expected key phrase appears in the generated text), citation correct (a cited page really contains the answer string), faithfulness (share of answer words that also appear in the retrieved context; low means made-up content) and correct refusal (out-of-document questions are refused).

Step 2: ingest and clean. clean() applies NFKC normalisation (so the ligature in the word classification becomes plain letters), re-joins words that were hyphenated at a line end, and collapses whitespace. load_pdf() opens a PDF, reads each page, cleans it and stores a record with the document key, the page number and the text. The page number is kept because it becomes the citation. All pages go into a pandas DataFrame and a per-paper summary is displayed.
Step 2: ingest and cleanIn [4]
def clean(text: str) -> str:
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text)          # 'ﬁ' -> 'fi'
    text = re.sub(r"-\n(?=[a-z])", "", text)            # re-join hyphenated line breaks
    text = re.sub(r"\s*\n\s*", " ", text)               # newlines -> spaces
    text = re.sub(r"\s{2,}", " ", text)
    return text.strip()

def load_pdf(key):
    pages = []
    for i, page in enumerate(fitz.open(f"{PDF_DIR}/{key}.pdf"), start=1):
        t = clean(page.get_text())
        if len(t) > 80:                                  # skip blank / figure-only pages
            pages.append({"doc": key, "page": i, "text": t})
    return pages

PAGES = [p for key in PAPERS for p in load_pdf(key)]
df_pages = pd.DataFrame(PAGES)
df_pages["words"] = df_pages.text.str.split().str.len()
summary = df_pages.groupby("doc").agg(pages=("page", "count"), words=("words", "sum"))
display(summary)
print("\nSample (attention, page 5):\n", PAGES[4]["text"][:300], "...")

4.2 Tokens and chunks

Step 3: tokenise, remove stop-words, lemmatise. tokenize() lower-cases the text, extracts alphanumeric tokens with a regular expression, removes NLTK stop-words and one-letter tokens, and lemmatises the rest. The demo sentence shows the effect ("layers" becomes "layer"). This function feeds TF-IDF and BM25 only; the dense model reads raw text.
Step 3: tokenise, remove stop-words, lemmatiseIn [5]
STOP = set(stopwords.words("english"))
LEM = WordNetLemmatizer()

def tokenize(text: str):
    toks = re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())              # lowercase + regex tokeniser
    return [LEM.lemmatize(t) for t in toks if t not in STOP and len(t) > 1]

demo = "The encoder is composed of a stack of N = 6 identical layers."
print("raw    :", demo)
print("tokens :", tokenize(demo))
Step 4: chunking. chunk_fixed() slides a 500-character window with 100 characters of overlap. chunk_sentence() splits a page into sentences, packs them until 500 characters would be exceeded, and starts the next chunk with the last sentence of the previous one so that context is not lost. Both keep the page number and never cross a page. The cell builds both versions, prints size statistics and shows an example chunk.
Step 4: chunkingIn [6]
def chunk_fixed(pages, size=500, overlap=100):
    out = []
    for p in pages:
        t, step = p["text"], size - overlap
        for start in range(0, max(len(t) - overlap, 1), step):
            piece = t[start:start + size].strip()
            if len(piece) > 60:
                out.append({"doc": p["doc"], "page": p["page"], "text": piece})
    return out

def chunk_sentence(pages, size=500):
    out = []
    for p in pages:
        sents, cur = sent_tokenize(p["text"]), []
        for s in sents:
            if cur and sum(len(x) + 1 for x in cur) + len(s) > size:
                out.append({"doc": p["doc"], "page": p["page"], "text": " ".join(cur)})
                cur = [cur[-1]]                       # one-sentence overlap
            cur.append(s)
        if cur and len(" ".join(cur)) > 60:
            out.append({"doc": p["doc"], "page": p["page"], "text": " ".join(cur)})
    return out

CHUNKERS = {"fixed-500/100": lambda: chunk_fixed(PAGES, 500, 100),
            "sentence-500":  lambda: chunk_sentence(PAGES, 500)}
CHUNKS = {name: fn() for name, fn in CHUNKERS.items()}
stats = pd.DataFrame({n: pd.Series([len(c["text"]) for c in cs]).describe()[["count", "mean", "min", "max"]]
                      for n, cs in CHUNKS.items()}).T.round(1)
display(stats)
print("\nExample sentence-aware chunk:\n", CHUNKS["sentence-500"][20])

4.3 Evaluation set and vector representations

Step 5: evaluation set and metric functions. Loads the 30 questions from JSON and splits them into answerable and out-of-document groups. key() normalises text for matching, is_hit() defines a correct chunk, and evaluate() takes any ranking function and returns Recall@1, 3, 5 and MRR. Because every retriever is plugged into the same function, the comparison is fair. The last loop reports how many questions are answerable at all with each chunking (the upper bound for any retriever).
Step 5: evaluation set and metric functionsIn [7]
EVAL = json.load(open(f"{DATA}/eval_questions.json"))
key = lambda s: re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]", "", unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", s).lower())
ANSWERABLE = [q for q in EVAL if q["doc"]]
UNANSWERABLE = [q for q in EVAL if not q["doc"]]
print(len(ANSWERABLE), "answerable,", len(UNANSWERABLE), "out-of-document")
display(pd.DataFrame(ANSWERABLE)[["id", "doc", "q"]].head(6))

def is_hit(chunk, q):
    return chunk["doc"] == q["doc"] and key(q["answer"]) in key(chunk["text"])

def evaluate(rank_fn, chunks, ks=(1, 3, 5)):
    # rank_fn(question) -> list of chunk indices, best first
    rr, hits = [], {k: 0 for k in ks}
    for q in ANSWERABLE:
        ranked = rank_fn(q["q"])[:max(ks)]
        pos = next((i for i, ci in enumerate(ranked) if is_hit(chunks[ci], q)), None)
        rr.append(0 if pos is None else 1 / (pos + 1))
        for k in ks:
            hits[k] += pos is not None and pos < k
    n = len(ANSWERABLE)
    return {**{f"Recall@{k}": hits[k] / n for k in ks}, "MRR": float(np.mean(rr))}

# how many answerable questions have at least one chunk that could be a hit? (upper bound)
for name, cs in CHUNKS.items():
    ok = sum(any(is_hit(c, q) for c in cs) for q in ANSWERABLE)
    print(f"{name:14s} answer string present in some chunk for {ok}/{len(ANSWERABLE)} questions")
Step 6: three vector representations in one class. The Index class builds, for one list of chunks: a TF-IDF matrix (fed with our own tokens), a BM25 index and the dense MiniLM embedding matrix (unit length, 384 columns). It offers four ranking methods: rank_tfidf, rank_bm25, rank_dense and rank_hybrid, which fuses the BM25 and dense rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. One index is built for each chunking strategy.
Step 6: three vector representations in one classIn [8]
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import torch

DEVICE = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
EMB_MODEL = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", device=DEVICE)
print("device:", DEVICE, "| embedding dim:", EMB_MODEL.get_sentence_embedding_dimension())

class Index:
    """All representations for one chunking strategy."""
    def __init__(self, chunks):
        self.chunks = chunks
        texts = [c["text"] for c in chunks]
        toks = [tokenize(t) for t in texts]
        # TF-IDF
        self.tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(analyzer=lambda x: x)       # we feed pre-tokenised text
        self.X_tfidf = self.tfidf.fit_transform(toks)
        # BM25
        self.bm25 = BM25Okapi(toks)
        # Dense
        t0 = time.time()
        self.E = EMB_MODEL.encode(texts, batch_size=64, normalize_embeddings=True, show_progress_bar=False)
        self.embed_seconds = time.time() - t0

    def rank_tfidf(self, q):
        s = (self.X_tfidf @ self.tfidf.transform([tokenize(q)]).T).toarray().ravel()
        return list(np.argsort(-s))
    def scores_dense(self, q):
        v = EMB_MODEL.encode([q], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
        return self.E @ v                                          # cosine (vectors are unit length)
    def rank_dense(self, q):
        return list(np.argsort(-self.scores_dense(q)))
    def rank_bm25(self, q):
        return list(np.argsort(-self.bm25.get_scores(tokenize(q))))
    def rank_hybrid(self, q, k=60):                                # reciprocal rank fusion
        fused = Counter()
        for ranking in (self.rank_bm25(q), self.rank_dense(q)):
            for r, ci in enumerate(ranking[:100]):
                fused[ci] += 1 / (k + r + 1)
        return [ci for ci, _ in fused.most_common()]

INDEX = {name: Index(cs) for name, cs in CHUNKS.items()}
for n, ix in INDEX.items():
    print(f"{n:14s} chunks={len(ix.chunks):4d}  tfidf-vocab={len(ix.tfidf.vocabulary_):5d}  "
          f"embeddings={ix.E.shape}  embed-time={ix.embed_seconds:.1f}s")
Step 7: NumPy vs FAISS. Builds a FAISS inner-product index from the embedding matrix, runs the same question through FAISS and through NumPy, asserts that the top-3 ids agree, and prints the three retrieved chunks with their cosine scores and page numbers. This proves that the matrix product and the library do the same exact search.
Step 7: NumPy vs FAISSIn [9]
import faiss
ix = INDEX["sentence-500"]
faiss_index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(ix.E.shape[1])
faiss_index.add(ix.E.astype("float32"))

q = "How many parallel attention heads does the Transformer use?"
qv = EMB_MODEL.encode([q], normalize_embeddings=True).astype("float32")
D, I = faiss_index.search(qv, 3)
numpy_top = ix.rank_dense(q)[:3]
print("FAISS top-3 :", list(I[0]), "scores", np.round(D[0], 3))
print("NumPy top-3 :", numpy_top, "scores", np.round(ix.scores_dense(q)[numpy_top], 3))
assert list(I[0]) == numpy_top, "FAISS and NumPy disagree"

for r, ci in enumerate(I[0], 1):
    c = ix.chunks[ci]
    print(f"\n#{r}  [{c['doc']} p.{c['page']}]  cosine={D[0][r-1]:.3f}\n    {c['text'][:230]}...")

4.5 Refusal, generation and answer evaluation

Step 9: choosing the refusal threshold. Computes the best cosine score for every question, then scans thresholds from 0.10 to 0.70 and keeps the value with the highest accept/refuse accuracy. Draws a histogram of the two groups with the threshold line.
Step 9: choosing the refusal thresholdIn [12]
BEST = INDEX["sentence-500"]
top_ans = [BEST.scores_dense(q["q"]).max() for q in ANSWERABLE]
top_out = [BEST.scores_dense(q["q"]).max() for q in UNANSWERABLE]
cands = np.linspace(0.1, 0.7, 121)
def acc(t): return (sum(s >= t for s in top_ans) + sum(s < t for s in top_out)) / (len(top_ans) + len(top_out))
THRESH = float(cands[int(np.argmax([acc(t) for t in cands]))])
print(f"answerable   : mean top-1 cosine = {np.mean(top_ans):.3f}  (min {min(top_ans):.3f})")
print(f"out-of-doc   : mean top-1 cosine = {np.mean(top_out):.3f}  (max {max(top_out):.3f})")
print(f"chosen threshold = {THRESH:.2f}  ->  accept/refuse accuracy = {acc(THRESH):.1%}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.2))
ax.hist(top_ans, bins=12, alpha=.8, label="answerable", color="#c2410c")
ax.hist(top_out, bins=6, alpha=.8, label="out-of-document", color="#475569")
ax.axvline(THRESH, ls="--", color="k"); ax.text(THRESH + .01, ax.get_ylim()[1] * .85, f"threshold {THRESH:.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("top-1 cosine similarity"); ax.set_ylabel("questions"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(f"{FIG}/refusal_threshold.png"); plt.show()
Step 10: generation with FLAN-T5. Loads FLAN-T5-base, defines the prompt template and the function ask(): score all chunks, take the top 3, refuse if the best score is below the threshold, otherwise build the prompt, generate with beam search and attach the citations from the chunk metadata (not from the model). Three demo questions follow, one of them out of scope.
Step 10: generation with FLAN-T5In [13]
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM
GEN_NAME = "google/flan-t5-base"
gtok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(GEN_NAME)
gen = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(GEN_NAME).to(DEVICE).eval()

PROMPT = ("""Answer the question using only the context below. Be brief.
If the context does not contain the answer, reply exactly: I don't know.

Context:
{context}

Question: {question}
Answer:""")

def ask(question, index=BEST, k=3, threshold=THRESH):
    scores = index.scores_dense(question)
    order = list(np.argsort(-scores)[:k])
    top = [(index.chunks[i], float(scores[i])) for i in order]
    if top[0][1] < threshold:
        return {"answer": "I could not find this in the documents.", "sources": [], "refused": True, "score": top[0][1], "top": top}
    context = "\n\n".join(f"[{c['doc']} p.{c['page']}] {c['text']}" for c, _ in top)
    inputs = gtok(PROMPT.format(context=context, question=question), return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=1024).to(DEVICE)
    with torch.no_grad():
        out = gen.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=64, num_beams=4)
    ans = gtok.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True).strip()
    src = [f"{c['doc']} p.{c['page']}" for c, _ in top[:2]]
    return {"answer": ans, "sources": src, "refused": False, "score": top[0][1], "top": top}

for q in ["How many parallel attention heads does the Transformer use?",
          "What fraction of tokens is hidden in the masked language model objective?",
          "What is the capital city of France?"]:
    r = ask(q)
    print(f"Q: {q}\nA: {r['answer']}   {r['sources']}   (top cosine {r['score']:.2f})\n")
Step 11: evaluating full answers. Runs ask() on all 25 answerable questions and records whether the answer contains the expected phrase, whether a cited page really contains the answer, the faithfulness score and whether the system wrongly refused. Then it counts correct refusals on the 5 out-of-document questions and saves a CSV.
Step 11: evaluating full answersIn [14]
def faithfulness(answer, top):
    a = set(tokenize(answer)); ctx = set(tokenize(" ".join(c["text"] for c, _ in top)))
    return len(a & ctx) / len(a) if a else 1.0

rows = []
for q in ANSWERABLE:
    r = ask(q["q"])
    exp = key(q["expect"])
    correct = (not r["refused"]) and exp in key(r["answer"])
    cite_ok = any(is_hit(c, q) for c, _ in r["top"][:2])
    rows.append({"id": q["id"], "question": q["q"], "answer": r["answer"], "correct": correct,
                 "citation_ok": cite_ok, "faithfulness": faithfulness(r["answer"], r["top"]), "refused": r["refused"]})
ANS = pd.DataFrame(rows)
ref = [ask(q["q"])["refused"] for q in UNANSWERABLE]

print(f"Answer correct      : {ANS.correct.mean():.1%}  ({ANS.correct.sum()}/{len(ANS)})")
print(f"Citation correct    : {ANS.citation_ok.mean():.1%}")
print(f"Mean faithfulness   : {ANS.faithfulness.mean():.2f}")
print(f"Wrongly refused     : {ANS.refused.sum()}/{len(ANS)} answerable questions")
print(f"Correctly refused   : {sum(ref)}/{len(ref)} out-of-document questions")
ANS.to_csv(f"{FIG}/answer_results.csv", index=False)
display(ANS[["id", "answer", "correct", "citation_ok"]].head(12))
Step 12: error analysis. Prints, for each wrongly answered question, the expected answer, the model's answer and whether the evidence was in the top-2 chunks. This separates retrieval errors from generation errors.

bad = ANS[~ANS.correct]
print(f"{len(bad)} questions answered incorrectly\n")
for _, r in bad.iterrows():
    q = next(x for x in ANSWERABLE if x["id"] == r.id)
    print(f"Q{q['id']}: {q['q']}\n   expected : {q['expect']}\n   got      : {r.answer}\n   evidence in top-2 retrieved chunks: {r.citation_ok}\n")

5.4 Web demo

The same retrieval idea runs in the browser at askmargin.vercel.app. The site loads the four sample papers from the files exported in Step 13 (717 chunks as JSON and their embeddings as 16-bit numbers), embeds the user's question with the same all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model (in a Web Worker), ranks the chunks by cosine similarity and applies the same 0.24 refusal threshold. A user can also drop in their own PDF, which is processed on their device. One difference from the notebook: the website answers in an extractive way, returning the best-matching sentences with their page numbers and cosine scores, and does not run FLAN-T5; the generated answers of this report come from the notebook only. The "under the hood" panel shows each stage (index, query vector, cosine search, answer).

Chapter 6Results, Analysis and Conclusion

6.1 Retrieval results

Table 6.1: Retrieval quality on the 25 answerable questions (from retrieval_results.csv). Best value per column in bold.
Chunking Method Recall@1 Recall@3 Recall@5 MRR
fixed-500/100 TF-IDF 0.48 0.72 0.76 0.595
fixed-500/100 BM25 0.44 0.80 0.84 0.615
fixed-500/100 Dense (MiniLM) 0.36 0.60 0.68 0.465
fixed-500/100 Hybrid (BM25 + Dense, RRF) 0.44 0.72 0.80 0.591
sentence-500 TF-IDF 0.44 0.60 0.64 0.523
sentence-500 BM25 0.44 0.68 0.84 0.589
sentence-500 Dense (MiniLM) 0.36 0.60 0.80 0.511
sentence-500 Hybrid (BM25 + Dense, RRF) 0.52 0.80 0.88 0.665

The best single configuration is the hybrid retriever on sentence-aware chunks: Recall@1 0.52, Recall@3 0.80, Recall@5 0.88 and MRR 0.665. Three honest observations follow. (1) Sentence-aware chunking is not clearly better than fixed windows. BM25 on fixed chunks reaches Recall@3 of 0.80 while BM25 on sentence chunks reaches 0.68, and TF-IDF is also higher on fixed chunks; sentence chunks win only with the hybrid retriever and for Recall@5 with dense retrieval. With 25 questions one question equals 0.04, so most gaps between rows are within noise. (2) Dense retrieval alone was not better than keyword search: Recall@3 is 0.60 against 0.72 to 0.80 for TF-IDF or BM25 on fixed chunks. A likely reason is that many questions contain very specific tokens (numbers, names such as "FAISS") that keyword methods match exactly. (3) The hybrid combines both signals and is the most robust choice on sentence chunks.

Table 6.2: Chunk-size ablation: dense retrieval, sentence-aware chunking (from chunk_size_ablation.csv).
Target size (chars) Chunks Recall@1 Recall@3 Recall@5 MRR
250 1417 0.52 0.68 0.80 0.621
500 717 0.36 0.60 0.80 0.511
800 373 0.40 0.64 0.80 0.538
1200 232 0.32 0.56 0.72 0.447

The largest chunks (1200 characters) are worst. The smallest size (250 characters) is best for dense retrieval, but the trend is not monotonic (800 is above 500), which again points to the noise of a 25-question test.

6.2 Refusal and full-answer results

The best cosine score of the 25 answerable questions has mean 0.618 (minimum 0.459); for the 5 out-of-document questions the mean is 0.195 (maximum 0.237). The two groups do not overlap, and the chosen threshold of 0.24 gives an accept/refuse accuracy of 100%: all 5 out-of-document questions were refused and none of the 25 answerable ones was wrongly refused.

Table 6.3: End-to-end results (generator: dense retrieval, top-3 chunks, sentence-500, FLAN-T5-base).
Metric Result

Mean faithfulness (answer words found in the context) 0.95

6.3 Error analysis

Eight of the 25 questions were answered incorrectly (ids 1, 7, 8, 10, 12, 17, 22, 25). For every one of them the notebook reports that the evidence string was not in the top-2 retrieved chunks, so all eight errors begin in retrieval, not in the language model. The generator then did one of three things. It admitted ignorance (Q1, "I don't know", although the topic is the number of attention heads). Or it picked a plausible but wrong detail from the context (Q10 answered "340M", the size of the large BERT model, instead of 110M for the base model; Q22 answered "MAX-strategy" instead of MEAN; Q17 "RAG-Sequence Model" instead of BART). Or it answered only a part of the question (Q8 gave the hardware "8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs" but not "3.5 days"; Q25 gave a different speed-up figure). The faithfulness of 0.95 shows that the generator almost never used words that were absent from the context: its failures are "right text, wrong fact" caused by the wrong chunk reaching the prompt.

Citation accuracy (52%) is lower than answer accuracy (68%): four questions (11, 15, 19, 23) were answered correctly although the two cited chunks did not contain the stored answer string. The check is strict, so 52% is conservative, but the cited page is not always the page holding the evidence, which is why the website shows the retrieved passages next to the answer.

6.4 Limitations

  • Small test set. Twenty-five answerable and five unanswerable questions; one question is 4 percentage points, so differences between close methods are not statistically reliable.
  • Threshold tuned on the test questions. The value 0.24 was chosen with the same 30 questions it is evaluated on. The gap between the groups is wide (0.237 against 0.459), but the out-of-document questions are completely off-topic. Questions that are close to the document's topic yet unanswered by it are harder and were not tested.
  • Crude metrics. A hit needs the exact answer string, so differently worded evidence is a miss; faithfulness is only word overlap.
  • Small generator. FLAN-T5-base (250 M parameters) can pick a wrong number from the context.
  • One corpus. Four English NLP papers; tables, equations and two-column layouts can still hurt extraction.

6.5 Future work

Add a cross-encoder re-ranker for the top 10 candidates; use a stronger generator than FLAN-T5-base; add close-but-unanswerable questions and tune the threshold on a separate validation split; add OCR for scanned PDFs.

6.6 Conclusion

Askmargin is a complete RAG pipeline written in Python: PDF extraction and cleaning, tokenisation, stop-word removal and lemmatisation, two chunking strategies, TF-IDF, BM25 and dense embeddings, a NumPy and FAISS vector store with cosine similarity, a hybrid retriever, a similarity-based refusal rule and answer generation with FLAN-T5. On 30 hand-written questions over four public papers the best retriever (hybrid on sentence-aware chunks) put the answer chunk in the top 3 for 80% of the questions and in the top 5 for 88%. The full system answered 68% of the questions correctly, refused all 5 out-of-document questions without refusing any answerable one, and produced answers with 0.95 faithfulness to the retrieved text. The main lesson is that retrieval quality decides answer quality.
